title: Operate and perform routine maintenance on equipment and tools

lessons.title: Safe operation of farm equipment
lessons.html:
Safe operation of farm equipment

At supervisor level you are expected to operate equipment correctly and safely, check it before use, and make sure the people working with you do the same. The Occupational Health and Safety Act 85 of 1993 and its Driven Machinery Regulations require that machinery is safe, guarded and used only by trained, authorised people.

Typical equipment and tools

  • Hand tools: spades, hoes, pruning shears, knives, saws, hammers, spanners.
  • Power tools: brush cutters, chainsaws, angle grinders, drills, pressure washers.
  • Equipment: knapsack and boom sprayers, water pumps, generators, compressors.
  • Tractors and implements: mowers, ploughs, discs, trailers.

Before you start: the pre-use check

  1. Read the operator's manual or follow the farm's standard operating procedure.
  2. Check guards are in place and secure, especially PTO shaft covers and blade guards.
  3. Check fuel, oil, coolant and hydraulic levels.
  4. Check tyres, belts, chains, hoses and blades for wear and damage.
  5. Check controls, brakes, lights and emergency stops work.
  6. Put on the required PPE: hearing protection, eye protection, gloves, boots, and chainsaw chaps for chainsaw work.
  7. Clear the work area of people, animals, stones and obstacles.

If anything is faulty, tag the equipment out of use and report it. Never use unsafe equipment.

Safe operating rules

  • Use the tool only for the job it was designed for.
  • Never remove or bypass guards and safety switches.
  • Never carry passengers on a tractor unless there is a proper seat.
  • Keep loose clothing, hair and jewellery away from moving parts.
  • Stop the engine, remove the key and wait for all parts to stop before clearing blockages or adjusting anything.
  • Refuel only when the engine is off and cool, away from flames; no smoking.
  • Work across slopes carefully; tractors can roll over. Use a ROPS and seat belt where fitted.

lessons.title: Routine maintenance and record keeping
lessons.html:
Routine maintenance and record keeping

Routine maintenance keeps equipment safe, reduces breakdowns during busy seasons and makes it last longer. Breakdowns at planting or harvest can cost the farm far more than the maintenance would have.

Types of maintenance

TypeExamples
Daily (before and after use)Check levels, clean, grease, check tyres and blades
Periodic (by hours or calendar)Change oil and filters, replace belts and spark plugs, service as the manual says
SeasonalFull service before the season; clean, protect and store after the season
RepairsFixing faults found; done by a qualified mechanic if beyond routine work

Routine tasks

  • Cleaning: remove soil, plant material and chemical residue. Clean sprayers by triple rinsing at the wash bay, away from water sources.
  • Lubrication: grease all grease points (nipples) as listed in the manual. Wipe the nipple first so dirt is not pushed in.
  • Air filters: clean or replace; dusty farm conditions block them quickly.
  • Sharpening: keep blades, chains and cutting tools sharp. Blunt tools are dangerous and slow.
  • Tightening: check nuts, bolts and fittings.
  • Hand tools: replace cracked handles, remove rust, oil metal parts and store tidy.

Lock-out before maintenance

Before maintenance, switch off, remove the key or disconnect the spark plug lead or power supply, release stored pressure in hydraulics and sprayers, support raised implements on stands and never under a jack alone.

Waste

Collect used oil, filters and batteries in marked containers for proper disposal or recycling. Never pour oil onto the ground or into drains.

Records

Keep a logbook for each machine: date, hours, work done, parts used, problems and who did it. Use the records to plan the next service and to spot machines that break down too often.

Supervising others

Check that your team does pre-use checks, uses PPE and reports faults. Make sure only trained workers use each machine.

Key points

  • Do a pre-use check every time; tag out and report faulty equipment.
  • Never bypass guards; stop the engine and remove the key before clearing blockages.
  • Follow the manual for daily, periodic and seasonal maintenance.
  • Lock out and release stored energy before maintenance work.
  • Dispose of oil and filters properly and keep a logbook for each machine.

quiz.question: What should you do if a pre-use check finds a missing PTO guard?

options.text: Tag it out of use and report it
Ask a co-worker to watch the shaft

quiz.question: Before clearing a blockage on a machine, what must you do?

options.text: Wear gloves and reach in quickly
Stop the engine, remove the key and wait for parts to stop
Ask the operator to hold the clutch

quiz.question: Why wipe a grease nipple before greasing?

options.text: So dirt is not pushed into the bearing

quiz.question: How should used engine oil be handled?

options.text: Poured onto the farm road to settle dust
Collected in marked containers for proper disposal or recycling

quiz.question: Which law and regulations require machinery to be guarded and used by trained people?
